## Overview

`Rceattle` fits CEATTLE, a climate-linked, single- and multi-species age-structured stock assessment model (Holsman et al. 2016; Adams et al. 2022), using Template Model Builder (TMB). This vignette is the starting point for new users: it fits five single- and multi-species models to walleye pollock, arrowtooth flounder, and Pacific cod in the Gulf of Alaska and eastern Bering Sea. The workflow is:

1.  Install `Rceattle`

2.  Load `Rceattle` and associated excel data

3.  Fit assessment models:

-   model 1: single species, recruitment deviations as penalized fixed effects;

-   model 2: three single-species models fit jointly, recruitment deviations as penalized fixed effects;

-   model 3: model 2 with natural mortality estimated for each species;

-   model 4: model 3 with recruitment deviations as random effects;

-   model 5: multispecies, with time- and age-varying natural mortality due to predation.

4.  Compare models by AIC and Mohn's rho (retrospective analysis)

5.  Review plots of input data, diagnostics, and results.

## 1. Installation

Install `Rceattle` and its dependencies with:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Not run when the vignette is built: it would reinstall the package mid-render.
# Rceattle (pulls CRAN dependencies automatically; e.g. TMB, Matrix, dplyr)
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("afsc-assessments/Rceattle")

# Optional: TMBhelper provides richer optimization diagnostics.
# Rceattle falls back to plain nlminb + sdreport if it's not installed.
# devtools::install_github("kaskr/TMB_contrib_R/TMBhelper")
```

## 2. Data

Data from the 2018 Gulf of Alaska and 2017 eastern Bering Sea single- and multi-species assessments are bundled with the package:

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(Rceattle)
data("GOApollock") # Data for GOA-pollock (1-species) ?GOApollock for more information on the data 
data("BS2017SS") # Combined data for 3 species. ?BS2017SS for more information on the data 
data("BS2017MS") # Multi-species data: lower residual mortality (M1_base) for pollock ages 1-2
```

Plot the data with `plot_data()`:

```{r}
plot_data(GOApollock)
```

A data list can be written to Excel, edited there, and read back into `R`:

```{r, message = FALSE}
Rceattle::write_data(data_list = BS2017SS, file = "BS2017SS.xlsx")
mydata <- Rceattle::read_data( file = "BS2017SS.xlsx")
```

The first sheet (`meta_data`) and `?BS2017SS` describe the inputs and file structure.

## 3. Fit models

Models are fit with `fit_mod()`. Model 1 is a single-species fit to Gulf of Alaska pollock with no stock–recruit relationship. It has 8 fleets: 1 fishery, 6 surveys, and 1 fleet turned off (its data excluded from the likelihood; see `model_1$data_list$fleet_control`).

```{r, message = FALSE}
model_1 <- Rceattle::fit_mod(data_list = GOApollock,
                            inits = NULL, # Initial parameters = 0
                            estimateMode = 0, # Estimate
                            random_rec = FALSE, # No random recruitment
                            fit_control = fit_control(
                              phase = TRUE,
                              verbose = 1))
summary(model_1)
```


Model 2 fits three single-species models jointly (`msmMode = 0`, the default), with no stock–recruit curve and natural mortality fixed at the input values (`mydata$M1_base`). It has 7 fleets: 3 fisheries (one per species) and 4 surveys (see `mydata$fleet_control`).

```{r, message = FALSE}
model_2 <- Rceattle::fit_mod(data_list = mydata,
                            inits = NULL, # Initial parameters = 0
                            estimateMode = 0, # Estimate
                            random_rec = FALSE, # No random recruitment
                            msmMode = 0, # Single-species
                            fit_control = fit_control(
                              phase = TRUE,
                              verbose = 1))
summary(model_2)
```

Model 3 estimates natural mortality with `build_M1()`; `M1_model = "sex_age_invariant"` estimates a single M per species, constant across sex and age:

```{r, message = FALSE}
model_3 <- Rceattle::fit_mod(data_list = mydata,
                              estimateMode = 0, # Estimate
                              M1Fun = build_M1(M1_model = "sex_age_invariant"), # Estimate sex-invariant M)
                              random_rec = FALSE, # Penalized likelihood
                              msmMode = 0, # Single species mode
                              fit_control = fit_control(
                                phase = TRUE,
                                verbose = 1))
summary(model_3)
```

Model 4 treats recruitment deviations as random effects (`random_rec = TRUE`), starting from model 3's MLEs and skipping phasing to reduce run time:

```{r, message = FALSE}
model_4 <- Rceattle::fit_mod(data_list = mydata,
                              inits = model_3$estimated_params, # Start estimation at model 3's MLEs
                              estimateMode = 0, # Estimate
                              M1Fun = build_M1(M1_model = "sex_age_invariant"),
                              random_rec = TRUE, # Random recruitment
                              msmMode = 0, # Single species mode
                              fit_control = fit_control(
                                phase = FALSE,
                                verbose = 1))
summary(model_4)
```

Model 5 sets `msmMode = 1`, running in multi-species mode: it estimates time- and age-varying natural mortality from predation, following the MSVPA parameterization of [Magnusson (1995)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00179756).

```{r, message = FALSE}
model_5 <- Rceattle::fit_mod(data_list = BS2017MS,
                            inits = model_3$estimated_params, # Initial parameters from single species estimates
                            M1Fun = build_M1(M1_model = "sex_age_invariant"),
                            estimateMode = 0, # Estimate
                            niter = 3, # 3 iterations around population and predation dynamics
                            random_rec = FALSE, # No random recruitment
                            msmMode = 1, # MSVPA based
                            suitMode = 0, # Empirical suitability
                            fit_control = fit_control(
                              verbose = 1))
summary(model_5)
```

## 4. Reading the fitted object

`fit_mod()` returns an object of class `Rceattle`, with the standard S3 methods:

```{r}
summary(model_1)        # reference points, likelihood, convergence
coef(model_1)           # estimated parameters
head(vcov(model_1))     # covariance matrix (NULL when getsd = FALSE)
logLik(model_1)         # log-likelihood, holding its degrees of freedom
AIC(model_1)            # so stats::AIC() works
head(residuals(model_1))
head(as.data.frame(model_1))
```

`plot()`, `simulate()` and `profile()` dispatch on the fit too. The diagnostics
(`retrospective()`, `jitter()`, `self_test()`, `profile()`, `osa_residuals()`)
return their own classes, whose `print()` methods summarize the result. A data
list read by `read_data()` also prints and summarizes.

Derived quantities on their natural scale (biomass, `ssb`, `N_at_age`,
`M_at_age`, `sel_at_age`, reference points and the likelihood components) are in
`fit$quantities`. The estimated parameters are in `fit$estimated_params`, mostly
on a log scale, under abbreviated names that `parameter_dictionary()` explains:

```{r}
parameter_dictionary("R_log_sd")             # log_sd of recruitment -> sigma_R
parameter_dictionary(process = "selectivity")
```

Anything beginning `log_`, or ending `_log_sd`, needs `exp()` to reach the
quantity named in the dictionary's `natural` column.

`quantity_dictionary()` does the same for the reported quantities: what each
means, its units and dimensions, and whether `sdreport()` gives it a standard
error:

```{r}
quantity_dictionary("ssb_depletion")
quantity_dictionary(process = "reference_points")

# Everything that holds a standard error
dict <- quantity_dictionary()
dict[dict$se, c("quantity", "units")]
```

Units follow the model throughout: numbers-at-age are **thousands of fish** and
weight-at-age is **kg**, so their product is **mt**. `ssb` is *female*
spawning-stock biomass. Every per-recruit reference point (`SPR0`, `SPRlimit`,
`SPRtarget`) is defined only in single-species mode; on a multispecies fit the
model leaves them at zero, which is not an estimate of zero.

## 5. Compare models

Models can be compared by marginal or joint negative log-likelihood, AIC, and retrospective analysis. AIC cannot compare a penalized-likelihood fit against a marginal-likelihood fit.

```{r}
# Evaluate 1 model
AIC(model_1)                    # AIC, via the logLik() method
model_1$opt$objective           # Negative log-likelihood
model_1$quantities$jnll_comp    # Negative log-likelihood components

# Compare AIC across 3-species penalized likelihood models
sapply(list(model_2, model_3, model_5), AIC)

```

`report_tables()` collects what an assessment reports (the fit and its
likelihood decomposition, time series with uncertainty, reference points, and
fits to index and catch) into tidy tables, each with a `model` column so several
fits stack for comparison:

```{r}
tabs <- report_tables(list(pollock = model_1, three_species = model_2))
tabs
tabs$reference_points
```

Read the `basis` column of `reference_points` before quoting from it. A CEATTLE
fit leaves a plausible-looking *number* for reference points it never estimated:
`Ftarget` and `Flimit` sit at 1.0/yr unless the harvest control rule estimates
them, and in multispecies mode `SB0` is a placeholder until a no-fishing
projection derives it. `report_tables()` returns those cells as `NA`, with the
reason in `basis`.

`report_tables()` never runs a retrospective or a jitter; pass in the ones you
have and the matching sections appear:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
report_tables(model_1, retro = model_1_retro, osa = osa_residuals(model_1))
```

`standard_output()` relabels the result into the NOAA standardized assessment
output read by the `stockplotr` and `asar` packages. That standard describes one
stock, so a fit with more than one species needs `species` to pick the stock:

```{r}
head(standard_output(tabs, model = "pollock"))
head(standard_output(tabs, model = "three_species", species = 1))
```

`retrospective()` measures retrospective bias, returning a list of refit models and a data.frame of Mohn's rho values.

```{r, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
model_1_retro <- retrospective(model_1, peels = 7)

# `mohns` is long: columns Object, `Forecast year` (0 = terminal peel), N, then one
# column per species. Read the rho by name -- column 2 is `Forecast year`, not a rho.
rho <- subset(model_1_retro$mohns, Object == "biomass" & `Forecast year` == 0)
plot_biomass(model_1_retro$Rceattle_list,
             model_names = paste("Pollock; mohns =", round(rho[["Pollock"]], 3)))
```

## 6. Model plots and diagnostics

`Rceattle` plots hindcast and projection time series of biomass, SSB, recruitment, biomass consumed as prey, mortality-at-age, and depletion, with uncertainty. Time-series plots accept a list of models.

```{r}
model_list <- list(model_2, model_3, model_4, model_5)
model_names <- list("single-spp", "Single-spp M", "Single-spp M - RE", "Multi-spp")

# Biomass
plot_biomass(model_list, model_names = model_names, incl_proj = TRUE, add_ci = TRUE)

```

```{r}
# Recruitment
plot_recruitment(model_list, model_names = model_names, incl_proj = TRUE, add_ci = TRUE)

# SSB
plot_ssb(model_list, model_names = model_names, incl_proj = TRUE, add_ci = TRUE)

# Biomass depletion (total biomass / B0)
plot_depletion(model_list, model_names = model_names, incl_proj = FALSE, add_ci = FALSE)

# SSB depletion (female spawning biomass / SB0), the quantity a Tier 3 HCR
# compares against B40%
plot_ssb_depletion(model_list, model_names = model_names, incl_proj = FALSE, add_ci = FALSE)

```

Diagnostic plots cover selectivity and the fits to composition, index and catch data. Composition plots take a single model; selectivity, index and catch plots take one or more.

`plot_selectivity()` draws each fleet on age, or on length bin for a fleet whose `Selectivity_dimension` is `"Length"`. With one model, colour is the year, so time-varying selectivity reads as a fan; with several, colour separates the models and the fan moves to transparency.

```{r}
# Selectivity
plot_selectivity(model_2)

# Overlay models; `line_col` and `lwd` apply as in the other plotters
plot_selectivity(model_list, model_names = model_names, lwd = 2)

# Plot composition fit
plot_comp(model_2)

# Plot index
plot_index(model_list) # - All models

# Plot catch data
plot_catch(model_list)
```

Components of the fitted object, accessed with `$`:

-   `model_1$initial_params` - initial parameter values

-   `model_1$bounds` - parameter bounds

-   `model_1$map` - parameter map in factor form (`model_1$map$mapFactor`) or list form (`model_1$map$mapList`)

-   `model_1$estimated_params` - estimated parameters

-   `model_1$quantities` - derived quantities (SSB, biomass, selectivity, etc)

-   `model_1$data_list` - the input data

-   `model_1$run_time` - model run time

-   `model_1$obj` - the TMB makeadfun object.

-   `model_1$opt` - the fit_tmb optimization object.

-   `model_1$sdrep` - the TMB sdreport object.
